title: Absolute Values Completions and P Adic Numbers

items.title: Absolute values on a field
An absolute value is nonarchimedean exactly when every integer has absolute value at most one
items.strategy: Use the strong triangle inequality to bound every repeated sum of 1 by 1. For the converse, apply the binomial theorem to powers of x+y after scaling so the larger of |x| and |y| is 1, and then run the power trick against the polynomial growth of binomial coefficients.

items.title: Equivalent nontrivial absolute values
Two nontrivial absolute values induce the same topology exactly when one is a positive power of the other
items.strategy: Compare the neighborhoods {x: |x| < 1} for the two absolute values and prove that the conditions |x| < 1 and |x|' < 1 are equivalent. Then pick one element of value greater than 1, pass to logarithms, and use a rational comparison argument to force a common exponent for every nonzero element.

items.title: The p-adic absolute value on the rationals
The p-adic absolute value is nonarchimedean
items.strategy: Translate multiplicativity and the minimum inequality for the published valuation on Q into the multiplicative and ultrametric laws for |.|_p = p^{-v_p(.)}. Keep the normalization |p|_p = p^{-1} explicit throughout.

items.title: Ostrowski's theorem for the rationals
items.strategy: Split into the archimedean and bounded-on-integers cases. In the archimedean case, use base expansions and the power trick to force a common real exponent of the usual absolute value; in the bounded case, show there is a unique prime p with |p| < 1 and then recover the p-adic absolute value up to a positive power.

items.title: Places of the rationals
The product formula for the rationals
items.strategy: Write a nonzero rational number as a signed product of prime powers in lowest terms. Under the normalized representatives of the finite and infinite places, every nontrivial factor is explicit and all but finitely many are 1, so the total product collapses to 1 by direct cancellation.

items.title: Weak approximation for rational places
items.strategy: First build rational numbers that are very small at all chosen places except one. Then take the usual finite linear combination against the desired targets. The proof must stay finite-place-by-finite-place and must not appeal to adeles or to an unstated Chinese-remainder theorem for completions.

items.title: The field of p-adic numbers as a metric completion
The p-adic completion is a complete valued field
items.strategy: Use the Cauchy-sequence model of metric completion and prove that termwise addition, multiplication, and the extended absolute value are independent of representatives. Show every Cauchy sequence is bounded, and for a nonzero class show representatives are eventually bounded away from zero so reciprocals are well defined and continuous.

items.title: P-adic balls are clopen and intersecting comparable balls are nested
items.strategy: Use the ultrametric inequality to show every point of a ball can serve as a center. The same inequality makes the complement of a ball a union of balls and forces two comparable balls that meet to lie one inside the other.

items.title: The p-adic completion agrees with the fraction field of Z_p
items.strategy: Keep the completion model and the compatible-residue model distinct until the comparison map is proved. Send an integral Cauchy class to its eventually stable residues modulo p^n, prove representative independence and bijectivity on the integral part, and then invert powers of p to reach the whole field.

items.title: Z_p is the valuation ring of Q_p
items.strategy: Transport the inequality |x|_p <= 1 across the comparison isomorphism and identify it with the integral compatible-residue classes. Keep separate the valuation-ring description and the later algebraic-integral-closure warning.

items.title: The maximal ideal and residue field of Z_p
items.strategy: Once Z_p has been identified as a valuation ring with uniformizer p, apply the standard DVR structure: the unique maximal ideal is pZ_p, and reduction modulo that ideal recovers F_p from the first residue coordinate.

items.title: Every p-adic number has a unique digit expansion
items.strategy: Choose digits inductively by least residues modulo p^n and prove the resulting partial sums are Cauchy. Uniqueness comes from the first index at which two expansions differ, while the valuation gives the finite negative tail for a nonzero element of Q_p.

items.title: Q_p is locally compact and totally disconnected
items.strategy: Use the unit ball Z_p as the compact open neighborhood and scale to reach arbitrary closed balls. Total disconnectedness comes from the clopen-ball basis, which separates any two distinct points without invoking later topological group machinery.

items.title: Simple roots lift uniquely in Z_p
items.strategy: Treat this as the p-adic specialization of Hensel lifting, not as a second general Hensel theorem. Starting from f(a_0) congruent to 0 mod p and f'(a_0) nonzero mod p, construct the unique root congruent to a_0 mod p by the standard lifting argument over Z_p.

items.title: Newton's criterion in Q_p
items.strategy: Run Newton iteration a_{n+1} = a_n - f(a_n)/f'(a_n) under the inequality |f(a_0)|_p < |f'(a_0)|_p^2. Taylor expansion shows the valuations improve quadratically and that every competing root in the same source-stated ball must coincide with the limit.

items.title: Square criterion in Q_p for odd p
items.strategy: Write x = p^n u with u in Z_p^x. Necessity is immediate from valuations and reduction mod p. For sufficiency, reduce to the unit case and apply simple-root lifting to X^2 - u after checking that the residue of u is a square in F_p^x.

items.title: Square criterion in Q_2
items.strategy: Again write x = 2^n u with u odd. Necessity comes from the valuation parity and reduction modulo 8. For sufficiency, use the stronger Newton criterion on X^2 - u at the point 1, since the derivative is not a unit modulo 2 and the simple-root version is not enough.

title: Absolute Values Completions and P Adic Numbers -- Examples

items.title: A geometric series that is p-adically convergent and really divergent
items.strategy: Take a ratio whose p-adic absolute value is less than 1 but whose usual absolute value is greater than 1, compute the partial sums explicitly, and compare the two metrics on the same sequence.

items.title: The p-adic expansion of minus one
items.strategy: Sum the finite geometric progression -(1 + p + ... + p^n) = -((p^{n+1}-1)/(p-1)), rewrite it as the digit string with every digit p-1, and pass to the p-adic limit of the partial sums.

items.title: A square root of minus one in Q_5
items.strategy: Start from a simple root of X^2 + 1 modulo 5, lift it with either the simple-root corollary or Newton iteration, and record several initial 5-adic digits of the root.

items.title: There is no square root of p in Q_p
items.strategy: Apply the odd-p square criterion to the valuation of p itself and show that the parity obstruction already rules the equation out, without any appeal to order or sign arguments from the real place.

items.title: Simple-root lifting by digits and by Newton iteration
items.strategy: Work through one polynomial with a simple residue-class root modulo p, first by successive lifts modulo p^n and then by Newton iteration, and compare the two approximating sequences term by term.

items.title: Testing odd units for squareness in Q_2
items.strategy: Check several odd units modulo 8, apply the exact Q_2 square criterion, and use the results to separate units that look similar modulo 2 but differ modulo 8.

items.title: One rational sequence in the real and p-adic metrics
items.strategy: Choose a rational sequence whose real behavior and p-adic behavior differ sharply, prove the two convergence claims directly from the two absolute values, and identify the two distinct limits or failures of convergence.

items.title: Z_p is not the integral closure of Z in Q_p
items.strategy: Use countability of the algebraic closure of Z inside Q_p and uncountability of Z_p to show the two sets cannot coincide. This isolates the difference between topological closure, valuation ring, and algebraic integral closure.

items.title: Dirichlet series
Abscissae of convergence and absolute convergence for a Dirichlet series
Convergence at one point gives a right half-plane of holomorphy
items.strategy: If the series converges at s_0, regard a_n n^{-s_0} as the coefficient sequence and apply Abel summation to bound the tails uniformly on compact sub-half-planes to the right of Re(s_0). Then pass to local uniform convergence and holomorphy on that half-plane.

items.title: Absolute convergence gives a right half-plane of termwise differentiation
items.strategy: On every closed half-plane Re(s) >= Re(s_0) + epsilon, compare n^{-s} and (log n)^k n^{-s} with convergent numerical majorants. The Weierstrass M-test gives locally uniform convergence for the original series and for each differentiated series.

items.title: The absolute-convergence abscissa is at most one to the right of the convergence abscissa
items.strategy: The inequality sigma_c <= sigma_a is immediate. For the bound sigma_a <= sigma_c + 1, start from one convergent point, bound the weighted coefficients there, and compare with the convergent p-series sum n^{-1-epsilon} one unit to the right.

items.title: A Dirichlet series determines its coefficients
items.strategy: Assume the difference series is identically zero on a common absolute half-plane and choose the least index m with nonzero coefficient. Multiply by m^s and let real s tend to +infinity; the leading coefficient survives while the absolutely convergent tail tends to 0.

items.title: Abel summation expresses a Dirichlet series by its summatory function
items.strategy: Apply the already-published Abel summation formula to the finite partial sums with g(x) = x^{-s}. Keep the endpoint term explicit, then prove that it tends to 0 under the growth hypothesis A(x) = O(x^theta) before taking the improper limit.

items.title: Dirichlet-series multiplication is Dirichlet convolution
items.strategy: In a common half-plane of absolute convergence, expand the product as a double series and regroup by the integer k = mn. The coefficient is the finite divisor sum defining Dirichlet convolution, and absolute convergence justifies the reordering.

items.title: Multiplicative functions give Euler products in the absolute half-plane
items.strategy: For each finite set of primes, expand the finite product of local factors and identify the coefficients by unique factorization. Then let the finite prime set increase and use absolute convergence to pass to the limit without any unauthorized rearrangement.

items.title: Completely multiplicative functions give geometric Euler factors
items.strategy: In the absolute half-plane, every local factor is a geometric series with ratio f(p)p^{-s}. Summing those local series gives the reciprocal linear factors and keeps the nonvanishing of each denominator explicit.

items.title: Landau's theorem for Dirichlet series with nonnegative coefficients
items.strategy: Assume the boundary point s = sigma_c were regular. Expand the function around a real point c > sigma_c, interchange the finite nonnegative sums in the resulting double series, and run the argument backward to continue the original Dirichlet series absolutely to some real point left of sigma_c, contradicting the definition.

items.title: The logarithmic derivative of zeta is the Dirichlet series of the von Mangoldt function
items.strategy: Work in Re(s) > 1, where the Euler product and its logarithm are absolutely convergent. Differentiate the logarithmic prime-factor series termwise and regroup prime powers to recover the von Mangoldt coefficients.

items.title: The Mobius Dirichlet series is 1/zeta
items.strategy: Multiply the Dirichlet series for the constant-one function and the Mobius function, use the convolution identity E * mu = epsilon, and identify the resulting constant series with 1. The absolute half-plane is what licenses the product manipulation.

items.title: The divisor Dirichlet series is zeta squared
items.strategy: Use the published identity tau = 1 * 1 and the multiplication theorem for Dirichlet series. No new Euler-product argument is needed once the convolution formula is already available.

items.title: The Euler totient Dirichlet series is zeta(s-1)/zeta(s)
items.strategy: Use the published arithmetic identity phi = mu * id_1 and apply the multiplication theorem to the Mobius series and the shifted zeta series sum n^{1-s}. Keep the honest absolute-convergence region Re(s) > 2 in the statement.

title: Dirichlet Series and Euler Products -- Examples

items.title: Dirichlet series with equal and unequal abscissae
items.strategy: Exhibit one series whose convergence and absolute-convergence abscissae agree and another with a positive gap, and verify both claims directly from the definitions rather than from heuristic boundary pictures.

items.title: Finite coefficient multiplication for 1/zeta
items.strategy: Multiply finite initial coefficients of the constant-one and Mobius Dirichlet series, see the cancellation at each positive integer n > 1, and then interpret the limit as the reciprocal-zeta identity.

items.title: Recovering tau(n) from zeta(s)^2
items.strategy: Expand the square of the zeta series formally and regroup the pairs mn = k to see that the coefficient counts divisors. Then compare the resulting coefficient rule with the named divisor-counting function.

items.title: The local Euler factor for the totient Dirichlet series
items.strategy: Compute the prime-power values of phi and check directly that the resulting local factor matches the quotient of the local zeta factors for zeta(s-1)/zeta(s).

items.title: The Dirichlet series of the Liouville function
items.strategy: Use complete multiplicativity of the Liouville function to write its Euler product, simplify each local factor, and identify the result as zeta(2s)/zeta(s) on the common absolute half-plane.

items.title: Outside absolute convergence, formal Euler-product regrouping is not licensed
items.strategy: Compare an honest conditionally convergent Dirichlet series with the product or regrouping one would get by pretending absolute convergence. The point is logical, not numerical: without absolute convergence the finite-prime limits no longer control arbitrary rearrangements.

items.title: A boundary line need not behave uniformly for a Dirichlet series
items.strategy: Give a Dirichlet series with two boundary points on Re(s) = sigma_c that behave differently, so the existence of one convergent boundary point does not upgrade the whole line into a line of convergence.
